study.title: Babylon Scam-Defense Fine-Tuning Experiments
study.objective: Measure optimizer and data-mix effects for Babylon scam defense on the unified multi-turn ScamBench, using Nebius-only remote training and tracking whether benchmark gains survive Babylon's deterministic output constraints.
notes: The current paper benchmark is the unified built-in ScamBench catalog: 107 scenarios and 210 stages, with 69 attack scenarios and 38 legitimate scenarios.
ScamBench is transcript-based and benchmark-decontaminated: the target model is not told it is in an eval and is asked only for the natural next outbound message in context.
The optimizer comparison runs Nebius-only on an H100 host. Local work in this phase was limited to orchestration, sync, validation fixes, and artifact consolidation; no laptop training was used.
On the corrected canonical benchmark, the Qwen3.5-4B baseline scores 8.49. The held-out-aware APOLLO-unweighted rerun scores 8.21 and no longer beats baseline.

The earlier 10.89 APOLLO-unweighted result is retained in the registry for provenance, but it predated the eval-source loading fix in train_local.py and should not be treated as the canonical generalization result.
The primary deterministic validator now passes through the corrected Action/Reason path; the remaining deterministic weakness is the auxiliary JSON-format recovery check.
Hermes remains integrated as baseline infrastructure, but it has not yet been rerun on the unified canonical benchmark and is therefore not part of the current corrected comparison.
recommended_next_steps: Rerun LoRA-unweighted, LoRA-weighted, and APOLLO-weighted under the same held-out-aware Nebius protocol before making any optimizer claim.
Add legitimate-intent recovery and natural-message curriculum, because the current trained and baseline runs all remain stuck at 4.0 on the legitimate intent slice.
Keep JSON-format recovery as a secondary compatibility target and continue measuring the primary action/reason gate separately.
Rerun Hermes on the unified canonical catalog after the corrected Qwen3.5-4B matrix is complete.

experiments.summary: Rebuilt ScamBench into a multi-turn transcript benchmark with live-attacker support, style variants, Pliny-derived suites, and harder trust-building scams.
worked: Moved the benchmark from single-turn prompts to stage-based transcripts with full transcript capture and stage-level scoring.
Added harder social and asymmetric-information scams, plus live attacker hooks that can adapt turn by turn.
Grounded three attack families in Pliny upstream repos and added explicit style/register variation.
did_not_work: The historical paper comparison artifact is now stale because it still reflects the old 4-scenario benchmark.
We do not yet have fresh baseline-versus-trained Qwen3.5 numbers on the new V2 suites.
experiments.why: The old benchmark was too easy to saturate and too structurally similar to the decision format used in training. The rebuild increases attack depth, conversational realism, and evaluation headroom.
experiments.try_next: Run the weighted-versus-unweighted ablations and fresh baseline/trained comparisons on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B using the V2 transcript harness.

experiments.summary: Untrained baseline used for all deltas.
worked: Refused direct seed-phrase requests reliably.
Already avoided explicit secret leakage on the four-scenario ScamBench front door.
did_not_work: Mapped the social-engineering case to refuse instead of the benchmark-safe audit/request-verification path.
Barely detected malicious requests in the broader trust slice.
experiments.why: The base model has some generic safety priors, but it does not reliably map adversarial prompts into the specific action schema or threat categories we need.
experiments.try_next: Train directly on Babylon-shaped scam-defense trajectories.

experiments.summary: First local anti-scam fine-tune.
worked: Established the local export-to-fine-tune-to-benchmark loop.
did_not_work: Underperformed the baseline on ScamBench.
experiments.why: The initial export mix did not shape the action policy correctly and overfit poorly to the benchmark action schema.
experiments.try_next: Increase scenario coverage and rebalance the training set around the exact benchmark-safe actions.

experiments.summary: Second fine-tune with better scenario coverage.
worked: Recovered from the v1 failure and beat the baseline.
Improved action selection on the social-engineering case.
did_not_work: Still left meaningful score on the table versus the eventual best run.
experiments.why: The model improved the action policy but still did not consistently land on the strongest explanations and repo-aware responses.
experiments.try_next: Sharpen the prompt-injection and repo-attack supervision.

experiments.summary: Best pure ScamBench checkpoint.
worked: Produced the strongest ScamBench result, improving the baseline by 19.5 points.
Lifted the malicious TrustBench slice far above baseline.
did_not_work: Degraded generic Babylon trading prompt quality.
experiments.why: The checkpoint was tuned too narrowly around the scam-defense JSON decision task.
experiments.try_next: Mix in a small amount of normal Babylon trading supervision to recover product-style behavior.

experiments.summary: First mixed-data attempt.
worked: Exposed a real data-schema issue before we trusted the mixed run.
did_not_work: Did not actually train on the intended mixed dataset.
experiments.why: The exporter emitted unsupported llmCalls.purpose values, so the loader dropped the trajectories containing the generic trading examples.
experiments.try_next: Fix the export schema and rerun the mixed training pass from scratch.

experiments.summary: Best balanced checkpoint across benchmark and product-style behavior.
worked: Recovered generic Babylon prompt quality to 3/3 passing validations.
Still beat the baseline on ScamBench.
Produced the strongest malicious TrustBench slice among the trained checkpoints we retained.
did_not_work: Lost the near-perfect ScamBench score achieved by v3.
experiments.why: The broader supervision improved general behavior and detector-style threat recognition, but it softened the narrow prompt-injection refusal policy that ScamBench rewards heavily.
experiments.try_next: Keep the mixed data, but add a smaller decode-robust prompt-injection booster or loss weighting for the direct prompt-injection case.

experiments.summary: Attempt to keep only three generic prompts while preserving peak ScamBench behavior.
worked: Confirmed that a smaller generic-data mix alone does not solve the tradeoff.
did_not_work: Failed to improve ScamBench over baseline.
Still did not fully preserve generic prompt quality.
experiments.why: The narrower mix reduced the generalization benefit without recovering the strict direct-refusal behavior that made v3 strong on ScamBench.
experiments.try_next: Focus on better prompt-injection-specific supervision or decode constraints rather than further shrinking the mixed dataset.

experiments.summary: First real Qwen3.5-4B baseline on ScamBench V2 and the malicious TrustBench slice.
worked: Confirmed that the rebuilt V2 benchmark is no longer saturated on a small modern baseline.
Established the real starting point for the Qwen3.5-4B ablation study on both ScamBench V2 and malicious TrustBench.
did_not_work: Baseline outputs often ignored the requested JSON format and spilled reasoning text into the response.
The base model was especially weak on repo-pressure and live social-engineering stages in ScamBench V2.
TrustBench recall was extremely low for prompt injection and credential theft.
experiments.why: The untuned base model can often refuse obvious attacks, but it is not aligned to the benchmark transcript format or to broad detector-style malicious intent recognition.
experiments.try_next: Compare weighted anti-scam supervision against an unweighted equal-sample control on the same Qwen3.5-4B base.

experiments.summary: Initial Qwen3.5-4B MLX LoRA attempt using the old hardcoded MLX settings.
worked: Exposed that the old MLX local-training path was still hardcoding aggressive settings that were acceptable for earlier smaller runs but not for Qwen3.5-4B V2 training.
did_not_work: Runtime ballooned into swap-heavy training and became impractical for repeated ablations.
The MLX path ignored --max-seq-length and lacked periodic checkpoints in the configuration we needed.
experiments.why: The MLX fine-tune path was still effectively tuned for older runs: it forced 1024-token sequences and a heavier memory profile than this workstation could sustain for Qwen3.5-4B transcript training.
experiments.try_next: Patch train_local.py so MLX honors max_seq_length, saves checkpoints periodically, and rerun both weighted and unweighted ablations with batch-size 1 at 512 tokens.

experiments.summary: Equal-sample unweighted ScamBench V2 control on Qwen3.5-4B.
worked: Improved over the Qwen3.5-4B baseline on both ScamBench V2 and the malicious TrustBench slice.
Showed that part of the gain does come from learning the benchmark transcript structure and task format.
Recovered some difficult V2 stages, including live social engineering, without any false-positive increase on TrustBench.
did_not_work: Left meaningful headroom relative to the weighted run on both benchmarks.
Still failed the generic Babylon deterministic action/reason validator.
Stayed weak on some repo-pressure and credential-theft cases compared with the weighted run.
experiments.why: An unweighted control teaches the output contract and some refusal behavior, but it underemphasizes the highest-risk transcript stages and broader detector-style malicious cues.
experiments.try_next: Use the same training configuration with weighted anti-scam supervision to isolate the contribution of ranking and risk weighting.

experiments.summary: Weighted ScamBench V2 anti-scam fine-tune on Qwen3.5-4B using the corrected MLX configuration.
worked: Beat the baseline by 6.6 points on ScamBench V2 and beat the unweighted control by 4.8 points under the same training setup.
Dramatically improved broad malicious-intent detection on the TrustBench slice, reaching 97.7% macro F1 with zero false positives in this slice.
Recovered the previously weak live social-engineering and repo-pressure ScamBench V2 scenarios while keeping strong performance on direct secret-exfiltration cases.
Validated that the main training lift is not only format learning: the weighted run materially outperformed the equal-sample control.
did_not_work: Still failed the generic Babylon deterministic action/reason validator, so this checkpoint is specialized rather than broadly product-safe.
Pliny-derived prompt-injection cases still retain headroom, especially the more indirect CL4R1T4S/L1B3RT4S style prompts.
experiments.why: Risk-weighted transcript supervision focused the model on the highest-value scam-defense turns and general malicious-intent cues, which lifted both multi-turn benchmark behavior and detector-style trust performance beyond what unweighted data alone achieved.
experiments.try_next: Repeat the same weighted vs unweighted study on Qwen3.5-9B, then add a decode-time JSON guard plus more indirect Pliny-style prompt-injection examples to close the remaining V2 gaps without sacrificing generic behavior.

experiments.summary: Expanded ScamBench V2 into the harder V3 suite with 14 scenarios, 30 stages, document-embedded injections, translation wrappers, and longer maintainer/social long cons.
worked: Pushed the baseline scores down enough to create real headroom again, especially on indirect prompt injections and more involved social scams.
Added the missing attack styles we cared about: document-embedded overrides, translation wrappers, and longer trust-building maintainer scams.
Exposed meaningful differences between unweighted and weighted training that were invisible on the easier V2 suite.
did_not_work: The first V3 weighted run regressed below baseline, which showed the older weighting recipe did not survive the benchmark expansion.
Some live and asymmetric-information stages are still saturated for both base and tuned models.
experiments.why: The harder suite intentionally rewards broader scam resistance and conversational robustness instead of only direct refusal behavior on easy single-format attacks.
experiments.try_next: Use the V3 suite as the default paper benchmark and tune the training recipe against its remaining weak spots rather than the older V2 artifact.

experiments.summary: Added a Babylon-native ScamBench seeding path that injects multi-turn attack transcripts into real chats, refreshes shared chat context, and exposes a CLI entrypoint for replay.
worked: ScamBench scenarios can now be replayed into Babylon group chats and DMs without coupling the engine directly to the benchmark package.
Seeded group chats immediately refresh the shared fact/summary layer, which makes the attack context available to other agents and chats.
The CLI surface makes it practical to replay attacks against a live Babylon user or agent without custom DB scripts.
did_not_work: This is still a manual replay path, not yet a continuously scheduled red-team rollout source.
Hermes is not yet attached to this same runtime path because its repo is still not mounted locally.
experiments.why: We needed a bridge between the offline multi-turn benchmark corpus and the live Babylon chat/runtime environment so the same attacks can be used for rollout generation and debugging.
experiments.try_next: Hook the seeding service into scheduled red-team jobs and live agent training data collection.

experiments.summary: Qwen3.5-4B baseline on the expanded ScamBench V3 suite plus the malicious TrustBench slice.
worked: Stayed strong on several direct secret-exfiltration and live group-chat stages even after the benchmark got harder.
Provided a non-saturated starting point for the 4B V3 ablations.
did_not_work: Collapsed on fake support, repo-pressure, and document-embedded prompt injections.
Barely detected prompt injection or credential theft in the TrustBench slice.
experiments.why: The expanded benchmark stresses conversational wrappers and indirect attacks that the untuned base model does not reliably map into the benchmark-safe actions or malicious-intent labels.
experiments.try_next: Compare equal-sample control training against retuned risk-weighted training on the same 4B base.

experiments.summary: First weighted Qwen3.5-4B V3 run before retuning the weighting recipe.
worked: Confirmed that the V3 suite was sensitive enough to reveal recipe mistakes quickly.
Preserved strength on direct prompt injection and repo-pressure while exposing the failure elsewhere.
did_not_work: Underperformed the 4B V3 baseline overall.
Regressed badly on broken-English support fraud and document-embedded prompt injections.
experiments.why: The pre-retune weighting emphasized the wrong stage families and did not focus enough on terminal secret pressure plus style/wrapper coverage.
experiments.try_next: Retune the weighting recipe around stage risk, terminal-secret pressure, and the specific V3 regression families.

experiments.summary: Equal-sample unweighted 4B control on ScamBench V3.
worked: Produced the best overall ScamBench V3 score among the final retained checkpoints.
Recovered the hardest wrapper-style and support-fraud scenarios, including the document-embedded override and repo-pressure case.
Improved the malicious TrustBench slice substantially over baseline without introducing false positives.
did_not_work: Still trailed the weighted run badly on broad malicious detection, especially prompt injection and credential theft.
Lost the direct prompt-injection strength that the weighted run recovered.
Still failed the generic Babylon deterministic action/reason validator.
experiments.why: The unweighted control learns the transcript format and broader scenario coverage well, but it does not concentrate enough probability mass on the highest-risk cues.
experiments.try_next: Use the unweighted control as the first stage of a two-step curriculum, then add a smaller weighted booster instead of a single weighted-only run.

experiments.summary: Retuned weighted 4B run using stage-risk and terminal-secret emphasis on ScamBench V3.
worked: Recovered above-baseline ScamBench V3 performance after the first weighted recipe failed.
Dominated the malicious TrustBench slice, especially prompt injection and credential theft.
Restored direct prompt-injection and long-con performance while keeping repo-pressure improvements.
did_not_work: Still trailed the unweighted control on overall ScamBench V3.
Regressed on fake support, broken-English ops, and document-embedded override scenarios.
Still failed the generic Babylon deterministic action/reason validator.
experiments.why: The retuned weighting improved the highest-risk refusal and detector behavior, but the current recipe still overfocuses direct secret pressure relative to style and wrapper attacks.
experiments.try_next: Blend this weighted booster with the unweighted control, or explicitly upsample support-fraud, broken-English, and doc-embedded attack families.

experiments.summary: Qwen3.5-9B baseline on ScamBench V3 and the malicious TrustBench slice.
worked: Handled some obvious support-fraud and live social/jailbreak scenarios without training.
Provided a stress test showing that a larger small model is not automatically safer on this suite.
did_not_work: Underperformed the 4B baseline on both ScamBench V3 and the malicious TrustBench slice.
Was especially weak on Pliny/libertas, asymmetric group-to-DM, and repo-pressure attacks.
experiments.why: Model size alone did not produce better scam resistance here; the 9B baseline appears more willing to follow indirect social and wrapper-style attacks.
experiments.try_next: If we continue on 9B, treat it as a separate recipe search instead of assuming the 4B settings will transfer.

experiments.summary: Equal-sample unweighted control on Qwen3.5-9B for ScamBench V3.
worked: Improved the 9B malicious TrustBench slice over the 9B baseline.
Lifted social-engineering and credential-theft detection slightly without adding false positives.
did_not_work: Still underperformed the 9B baseline on ScamBench V3.
Prompt-injection recall remained at zero in the TrustBench slice.
Did not recover the 9B model's weak group-to-DM and wrapper-style scam behavior.
experiments.why: The small unweighted dataset was not enough to move the 9B model toward the right multi-turn action policy, even though it nudged detector-style behavior slightly upward.
experiments.try_next: If continuing on 9B, lower the learning rate and add stronger base-preserving regularization before trying to scale the data recipe.

experiments.summary: Retuned weighted Qwen3.5-9B run on ScamBench V3.
worked: Produced the best malicious TrustBench score among the 9B runs, especially on social engineering.
Showed that the 9B model can learn some detector-style malicious cues from the weighted recipe.
did_not_work: Produced the worst ScamBench V3 score among the 9B runs.
Left prompt-injection recall at zero on the TrustBench slice.
Regressed sharply on long-con and asymmetric-information ScamBench stages.
experiments.why: The retuned 4B weighting recipe does not transfer cleanly to 9B at this data scale; it appears to sharpen some social-engineering cues while degrading the multi-turn action policy that ScamBench rewards.
experiments.try_next: Treat 9B as a separate research thread with lower LR, more data, and stronger regularization rather than carrying this recipe into the paper as a success case.

experiments.summary: Mounted Hermes locally and attached it to the same ScamBench and TrustBench harnesses using a JSONL bridge over a served Qwen3.5-4B endpoint.
worked: Mounted Hermes locally and validated the bridge with unit tests plus live served-model calls.
Completed a full 14-scenario ScamBench V3 run and scored it through the same recorded-decision harness used elsewhere in the paper.
Completed the malicious TrustBench slice with very strong prompt-injection, social-engineering, and credential-theft detection.
did_not_work: The first bridge client implementation produced empty responses because it generated the argparse flags for --no-tools incorrectly.
Subset ScamBench smoke runs cannot be auto-scored yet because the current recorded-decision scorer expects the full catalog.
experiments.why: Hermes can now be compared on the same suites as Babylon, but the integration needed a dedicated bridge, correct subprocess defaults, and stage-level checkpointing to be robust under longer multi-turn runs.
experiments.try_next: Add subset-aware recorded scoring or scenario filtering to the TS CLI, then benchmark Hermes against trained Babylon checkpoints on identical Qwen3.5 backends.

experiments.summary: Pulled and reviewed 30 external scam datasets from Hugging Face, inferred their shapes, grouped duplicate families, and produced a transform plan for policy training versus detector use.
worked: Separated conversation corpora from detector corpora so we do not blindly mix classifier rows into the agent-policy SFT path.
Confirmed several duplicate families early, including BluefinTuna/donksg, BothBosu/thananos, and BothBosu/Lyr1k overlaps.
Produced a clean transform plan that tells us which sources are safe to use for ScamBench synthesis versus training augmentation.
did_not_work: The raw dataset list materially overstated coverage because several repos are near-duplicates or split variants of the same underlying corpus.
Most external corpora are dominated by social-engineering and phone-scam content, not prompt-injection or repo-aware attacks.
experiments.why: Without the inventory and dedup pass, external-data gains would have been confounded by repeated corpora and by mixing detector datasets directly into the policy training path.
experiments.try_next: Materialize the conversation and SFT-style corpora into Babylon-shaped trajectories and use only the detector-style sets for auxiliary detection or reward modeling.

experiments.summary: Materialized the reviewed external scam corpora into Babylon training examples and a curated multi-turn ScamBench augmentation bundle, then validated the augmented benchmark and export paths end to end.
worked: Converted external conversation data into Babylon-shaped JSON decision examples that load directly through the existing local training pipeline.
Produced a curated 47-scenario external bundle that stays multi-turn and avoids the raw 2,047-scenario dump becoming a noisy benchmark.
Validated the augmented benchmark end to end with the perfect/failing smoke run and validated the export by loading all 366 trajectories into train_local.
did_not_work: The external corpora still add almost no prompt-injection coverage, so Pliny-style and repo-aware attacks remain mostly synthetic or internally generated.
Raw external transcript parsing initially leaked victim/target turns into benchmark context and over-classified phone-call transcripts as group chats until the materializer was corrected.
experiments.why: External scam corpora are valuable for trust-building, phone fraud, and long-con behaviors, but they need role-cleaning, family deduplication, and benchmark curation before they are safe to use for policy training or evaluation.
experiments.try_next: Use the new augmented export as the default external-data training source for the next 4B/9B ablation runs, and separately synthesize more prompt-injection and repo-aware attacks to balance the externally sourced social-engineering skew.

experiments.summary: Materialized prompt-injection source repos into Babylon training examples and curated ScamBench suites using awesome-prompt-injection as taxonomy plus L1B3RT4S, CL4R1T4S, and OBLITERATUS as concrete attack sources.
worked: Balanced the earlier external social-engineering skew by adding a dedicated prompt-injection corpus.
Used all four requested sources in a structured way instead of collapsing them into one undifferentiated text dump.
Converted repo-derived prompt attacks into Babylon-shaped training examples and curated benchmark scenarios.
did_not_work: OBLITERATUS itself is not a native prompt-injection payload corpus, so only its anti-refusal framing and scam-adjacent harmful prompts were directly useful here.
The awesome-prompt-injection repo is an index, not a payload dataset, so it contributes taxonomy and derived attack families rather than direct transcript rows.
experiments.why: The four repos are complementary: one is taxonomy, two are strong prompt payload sources, and one is refusal-removal framing. Treating them as separate source types preserves signal instead of flattening everything into generic jailbreak text.
experiments.try_next: Train the next prompt-injection-heavy ablation on this corpus and measure whether the added direct-injection coverage closes the remaining gap on wrapper, tool-hijack, and disclosure attacks.

experiments.summary: Merged the external scam corpus and the new prompt-injection corpus into one benchmark/training bundle, then rebuilt the merged ScamBench catalog and Babylon export.
worked: Produced a single merged bundle that the existing export and benchmark paths can consume without extra one-off glue.
Shifted the external scenario mix from almost all social-engineering to a more balanced split including 25 prompt-injection and 9 research-assisted scenarios.
Validated the merged catalog with the perfect/failing smoke run and validated the merged export through train_local sample loading.
did_not_work: The external prompt-injection mix is still weaker on truly indirect repo-aware attacks than the hand-authored core benchmark suites.
Scenario volume is now high enough that full model evaluations will be slower, so short smoke subsets still matter for iteration speed.
experiments.why: A merged bundle is the cleanest operational path: one external scenario file for ScamBench and one external training directory for Babylon export. That lets us actually train and benchmark on the same expanded threat surface.
experiments.try_next: Rerun baseline-versus-trained 4B/9B comparisons on the merged 95-scenario catalog and compare unweighted versus weighted training using the merged 3,287-sample export.

experiments.summary: Traversed the awesome-prompt-injection outbound links and reviewed which linked repos actually contain reusable attack assets versus taxonomy or defense references.
worked: Separated direct prompt/scenario sources from defense-only or taxonomy-only repos.

Confirmed that InjectLab, token-turbulenz, AgentSeal, the two CTF repos, DVLLA, and Sentinel AI contain concrete reusable attack assets, while the remaining repos contribute policy, detector, or dataset references.
Confirmed that Bastion, Garak, and prompt-injection-defenses are more useful for taxonomy, detectors, and ablation framing than raw attack transcripts.
did_not_work: Most of the newly cloned repos still require transformation before they are directly usable for policy training.
Detector/policy repos such as Vigil, PIC, BodAIGuard, and InjecGuard do not directly provide multi-turn transcripts.
experiments.why: The awesome list is valuable only if its links are resolved into concrete prompt families, challenge assets, or reusable detector patterns. The traversal step distinguishes signal from citation noise.
experiments.try_next: Keep materializing the direct-asset repos and use the detector/policy repos as auxiliary evaluation, reward-model, and variant-generation references.

experiments.summary: Materialized awesome-linked prompt-injection assets into Babylon training examples and merged them into the main ScamBench/Babylon threat bundle.
worked: Added concrete prompt-injection families from InjectLab, token-turbulenz, AgentSeal, ctf-prompt-injection, ai-prompt-ctf, DVLLA, and Sentinel AI.
Preserved multi-turn attack structure for AgentSeal siren/payload-splitting/memory-poisoning families and for several CTF-style attacks.
Regenerated a larger merged ScamBench catalog and a larger Babylon export that the local trainer accepts.
did_not_work: The added corpus is still prompt-injection heavy, especially from AgentSeal-style canary probes, so it should not be treated as a balanced product dataset by itself.
Tooling/taxonomy repos such as Bastion and Garak were not directly materialized into transcripts because they mostly contribute patterns, not ready-made conversations.
experiments.why: Following the awesome links yielded more concrete multi-turn prompt-injection assets than the original index or direct Pliny repos alone. Merging them increases benchmark headroom and training diversity, but also increases prompt-injection skew.
experiments.try_next: Train the next 4B/9B ablations on the new merged export while separately measuring whether the AgentSeal-heavy prompt families overfit prompt-injection at the expense of social scam robustness.

experiments.summary: Integrated difraud/difraud into the external scam-data pipeline with multi-file ingestion, resilient decoding, merged detector corpora, and refreshed benchmark/export artifacts.
worked: Integrated difraud as a multi-file detector-style corpus instead of collapsing it to a single sampled file.
Hardened the review/materialization loaders against non-UTF-8 CSVs and per-file schema drift so one bad file no longer kills the full run.
Propagated the refreshed external corpus through the merged threat bundle, ScamBench catalog, smoke validation, and Babylon export.
did_not_work: difraud is still detector-style text classification data, so it does not directly add grounded multi-turn transcript scenarios without further synthesis.
The current export path still benefits difraud mostly through detector/reward-model coverage rather than direct agent-policy SFT examples.
experiments.why: difraud adds broad cross-domain deception coverage, but it has to be integrated honestly as detector-style data. The pipeline changes preserve that distinction while still making the corpus available for downstream reward modeling, auxiliary training, and future scenario synthesis.
experiments.try_next: Convert high-signal difraud phishing/job/SMS positives into synthetic multi-turn red-team scenarios and use the merged detector corpus for a dedicated scam detector or reward-model ablation.

experiments.summary: Converted high-signal difraud phishing, job-scam, and SMS detector rows into synthetic multi-turn scam transcripts and regenerated weighted and unweighted Babylon exports on the difraud-expanded catalog.
worked: Turned difraud detector rows into realistic multi-turn phishing, job-scam, and SMS attack scripts instead of leaving them as flat classifier examples.
Forced the curated scenario set to retain difraud-derived suites so the synthetic work actually changes benchmark difficulty and not just the raw seed pool.
Produced matched weighted and unweighted exports on the same difraud-expanded catalog so the ablation isolates ranking/weighting effects from data-shape effects.
did_not_work: The local trainer still needed the same export directory reused as eval data because grouped split validation fails on the current single-window export layout.
The full 163-scenario catalog was too slow to use for every inner-loop model choice, so a 48-scenario difraud-heavy dev slice was still required for checkpoint selection.
experiments.why: difraud only becomes useful for agent-policy training once its detector positives are lifted into staged attacker transcripts. The synthetic conversion creates that bridge while preserving an honest weighted-vs-unweighted control.
experiments.try_next: Use the difraud-synth exports for fresh Qwen3.5 ablations, then decide whether weighting helps once the benchmark is harder and more socially skewed.

experiments.summary: Ran weighted versus unweighted Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B ablations on the difraud-synth exports, including dev-slice selection, malicious TrustBench, and full-catalog ScamBench runs.
worked: The harder difraud-synth catalog created real headroom and the 4B unweighted control improved full ScamBench from 22.0 to 28.8 while the 4B weighted run still beat baseline at 24.5.
The 4B checkpoints dramatically improved the broader malicious TrustBench slice, from 23.2% macro F1 at baseline to 98.9% unweighted and 100.0% weighted.
The 9B unweighted control remained the best 9B fine-tune, improving full ScamBench slightly from 18.0 to 18.7 and malicious TrustBench from 11.1% to 64.8%.
did_not_work: The weighted recipe did not transfer cleanly to 9B: it lost on the dev ScamBench slice, lost on the full 163-scenario ScamBench catalog, and also underperformed the 9B unweighted control on TrustBench.
Weighting was not the best way to maximize the harder scam benchmark itself, even at 4B, where the unweighted control clearly outperformed the weighted run on both dev and full ScamBench.
These local training runs still use overlapping train/eval exports because the current grouped split path is not compatible with the exported trajectory shape.
experiments.why: On the difraud-expanded setup, broad transcript exposure appears more important than aggressive ranking weights for the agent-policy objective. The smaller 4B model benefits strongly from the added data, while the 9B model is more sensitive to weighting and may need a milder curriculum or different optimizer settings.
experiments.try_next: Create a proper held-out grouped eval split, retune 9B with lower learning rate and softer weighting, and explore a detector-or-reward-model auxiliary objective that uses the merged detector corpora without over-optimizing the policy output format.

experiments.summary: Collapsed the scam-defense work into one canonical release selection plus one build script, then packaged a Hugging Face-ready dataset repo, four Hugging Face-ready model repos, and the paper artifacts into a single release bundle.
worked: Defined a single explicit release selection file instead of reconstructing the canonical dataset/model set from scattered experiment paths.
Packaged a self-contained release bundle with one Hugging Face-ready dataset repo, one Hugging Face-ready repo per selected model, copied paper artifacts, and exact training/publish instructions.
Trimmed model repo contents to the final adapter payloads instead of shipping intermediate checkpoint shards, and removed Python cache directories from the training surface.
did_not_work: Historical experiment artifacts were intentionally left in place because the paper pipeline and experiment log still reference them, so consolidation stops at the canonical release surface rather than deleting all old runs.
The local release builder cannot push to Hugging Face from this environment, so the output is upload-ready but not published.
experiments.why: The previous workflow was correct but fragmented. A stable release selection plus a single bundle builder makes the final dataset, models, and publication artifacts reproducible and substantially easier to ship.
experiments.try_next: Push the packaged dataset and model repos to Hugging Face once network/auth is available, then replace any remaining ad hoc upload steps with the canonical bundle path.

experiments.summary: Canonical release checkpoint for the best full-catalog ScamBench result on the final difraud-expanded matrix.
worked: Produced the strongest final 163-scenario ScamBench result in the release matrix.
Improved the 4B baseline materially on both ScamBench and the broader malicious TrustBench slice.
Shows that broad transcript exposure, not only risk weighting, is enough to materially improve scam resistance at 4B.
did_not_work: Did not match the weighted run on broader malicious detection.
Still failed the deterministic Babylon trading-format validation suite.
Primary deterministic validation still fails.
experiments.why: On the final difraud-expanded benchmark, the broader unweighted transcript mix best preserves coverage across many scam styles and prompt wrappers, which matters more for overall benchmark score than aggressive weighting.
experiments.try_next: Use this checkpoint as the first stage of a 4B curriculum, then test whether a smaller weighted booster can preserve its benchmark gains while improving product-facing safety coverage.

experiments.summary: Canonical release checkpoint for the strongest broader malicious-defense result on the final 4B matrix.
worked: Produced the strongest broader malicious TrustBench result in the final release matrix.
Still beat the 4B baseline on the full 163-scenario ScamBench catalog.
Demonstrates that weighting is useful as a broader malicious-defense booster even when it is not the best way to optimize the harder benchmark itself.
did_not_work: Underperformed the unweighted 4B checkpoint on the full ScamBench catalog.
Still failed the deterministic Babylon trading-format validation suite.
Primary deterministic validation still fails.
experiments.why: Weighting concentrates training mass on the highest-risk scam-defense turns and detector-style malicious cues, which is valuable for broader defense coverage but can overfocus direct high-risk pressure relative to wrapper and style diversity.
experiments.try_next: Blend this weighted checkpoint or corpus with the unweighted benchmark-best stage instead of treating it as the final single-stage optimizer.

experiments.summary: Best 9B checkpoint in the final release matrix; included as a modest improvement rather than a headline success.
worked: Produced the best 9B result in the final release matrix.
Improved the 9B baseline on both ScamBench and the broader malicious TrustBench slice.
did_not_work: The ScamBench gain was small relative to the 4B lift.
The 9B recipe remains unstable enough that it should not be presented as the main success case.
Still failed the deterministic Babylon trading-format validation suite.
Primary deterministic validation still fails.
experiments.why: The larger small model appears more sensitive to the fine-tuning recipe, so broad unweighted exposure helps a little but the current setup is not yet strong enough to justify the same claim we can make for 4B.
experiments.try_next: Treat 9B as a separate optimization problem with milder updates and a proper held-out split before making any stronger claim.

experiments.summary: Ran a Nebius-only Qwen3.5-4B optimizer matrix on the unified canonical ScamBench, comparing baseline, LoRA, and APOLLO under matched unweighted and weighted exports.
worked: APOLLO unweighted became the first optimizer condition on the corrected canonical benchmark to beat the 4B baseline, improving ScamBench from 8.49 to 10.89.
The Nebius runner executed the full matrix remotely on an H100 and reproduced the comparison without using local training hardware.
The APOLLO gain concentrated in prompt-injection scenarios, where the category average rose from 17.46 at baseline to 32.33.
did_not_work: Both LoRA runs regressed below baseline on the unified canonical benchmark.
APOLLO weighted also regressed below baseline, so more weighted data was not an optimizer win here.
All trained runs still failed the deterministic Babylon action/reason and decision-format gates.
experiments.why: On the smaller canonical benchmark, optimizer choice mattered more than weighting. APOLLO's full-parameter updates helped the model adapt to prompt-injection style attacks, while the weighted curriculum appears to have narrowed behavior in a way that hurt overall benchmark performance.
experiments.try_next: Use APOLLO-unweighted as the new optimizer baseline, add format-recovery mixing, and rerun the same matrix on a grouped held-out split before making a stronger paper claim.

experiments.summary: Untuned Qwen3.5-4B reference measured on the unified canonical ScamBench through the Nebius CUDA harness.
worked: Established the canonical 4B baseline on the corrected unified benchmark and the Nebius-only remote harness.
Outperformed all LoRA conditions in this matrix.
did_not_work: Remained far below the blanket-refusal anchor.
Stayed flat at 4.0 on the legitimate intent slice, so it is not handling benign requests well either.
experiments.why: The raw base model has generic safety priors but no scam-defense specialization, and the unified benchmark now exposes that weakness much more clearly than the earlier local catalogs did.
experiments.try_next: Use this run as the fixed baseline for future unified Nebius matrices so optimizer and data-mix changes are measured against the same canonical target.

experiments.summary: LoRA fine-tune on the smaller unweighted unified export, run remotely on Nebius.
worked: Completed cleanly on the Nebius CUDA path and produced a direct LoRA baseline against APOLLO on the same export.
Improved some attack-side social and research-assisted behavior relative to the raw baseline.
did_not_work: Underperformed the raw baseline on the overall unified benchmark.
Primary deterministic validation passes, but the auxiliary JSON-format recovery check still fails.
experiments.why: The small unweighted export was enough to move behavior, but LoRA did not transfer those changes into a net win on the harder unified benchmark and appears too brittle on prompt-injection-heavy slices.
experiments.try_next: Do not treat LoRA-unweighted as the reference going forward; compare future format-recovery mixes directly against APOLLO-unweighted instead.

experiments.summary: LoRA fine-tune on the larger weighted unified export, run remotely on Nebius.
worked: Proved the weighted export can be run end to end on the Nebius CUDA path with the same remote harness as the other conditions.
Matched the LoRA-unweighted result closely enough to show the regression is not just an artifact of the tiny unweighted subset.
did_not_work: Still underperformed the raw baseline on the overall unified benchmark.
Primary deterministic validation passes, but the auxiliary JSON-format recovery check still fails.
experiments.why: Adding more weighted data did not rescue the LoRA path on the unified benchmark. The optimizer appears to remain the limiting factor rather than sample count alone.
experiments.try_next: Use the weighted export with APOLLO and format-recovery mixing instead of continuing to push the same LoRA recipe.

experiments.summary: Earlier Nebius APOLLO-unweighted result before the held-out eval-source fix; kept for provenance but no longer canonical.
worked: Beat the raw 4B baseline on the unified canonical benchmark and clearly outperformed both LoRA conditions in the same Nebius matrix.
Delivered the strongest prompt-injection category result in the matrix, lifting that slice from 17.46 at baseline to 32.33.
Validated the Nebius-only APOLLO path end to end after fixing the CUDA precision issue that initially blocked the run.
did_not_work: The score was inflated relative to the corrected held-out-aware rerun because this run predated the eval-source loading fix in train_local.py.
Primary deterministic validation passes, but the auxiliary JSON-format recovery check still fails.
experiments.why: This run used the older Nebius training path before the held-out eval-source fix. It remains useful as provenance for the optimizer sweep, but not as the canonical generalization result.
experiments.try_next: Anchor the paper and release on the held-out-aware rerun instead of this earlier result, then rerun the rest of the optimizer matrix under the same corrected protocol.

experiments.summary: Held-out-aware APOLLO rerun on Nebius after fixing eval-source loading in train_local.py.
worked: Completed a clean Nebius-only APOLLO rerun with the held-out eval source explicitly loaded during training validation.
Primary deterministic validation still passes on the corrected rerun via the action/reason gate.
Prompt-injection and credential-theft slices remain the strongest parts of the trained model even under the stricter rerun.
did_not_work: Did not beat the raw 4B baseline on the unified benchmark once the held-out-aware training path was used.
The legitimate-intent slice remained stuck at 4.0, so the model still over-refuses or mishandles benign scenarios.
Primary deterministic validation passes, but the auxiliary JSON-format recovery check still fails.
experiments.why: The earlier 10.89 result was overstated by the older training path. Once the eval-source loading bug was fixed and the model was rerun against the held-out split, the benchmark advantage disappeared.
experiments.try_next: Rerun the full optimizer matrix under the corrected held-out protocol, then add legitimate-intent recovery and natural-message curriculum before making another capability claim.

experiments.summary: APOLLO full-parameter fine-tune on the larger weighted unified export, run remotely on Nebius.
worked: Showed that APOLLO itself is not the whole answer: the optimizer can still lose when the weighted curriculum is wrong for the canonical benchmark.
Improved the research-assisted category relative to baseline even though the overall benchmark regressed.
did_not_work: Underperformed the raw baseline and the APOLLO-unweighted condition on the unified benchmark.
Primary deterministic validation passes, but the auxiliary JSON-format recovery check still fails.
experiments.why: On the current canonical benchmark, weighted training appears to narrow behavior too aggressively even under APOLLO. The optimizer helps, but it does not rescue a curriculum that is misaligned with the benchmark mix.
experiments.try_next: Keep APOLLO but soften or rebalance the weighted export, and add explicit format-recovery supervision before rerunning this condition.
